source.drive: AMAF 2026 6(Plenary: Retention through safe, supportive, accountable workplaces. Data-driven deployment & Plenary: Scaling-up the implementation of the Global PPHF Guidelines Day 2 Wrap-Up & Synthesis )

segments.text: I'm just seeing a few more people in the back, let me take your seats. All right, so good afternoon again colleagues, thank you again for all the productive discussion and conversation as we continue into the discussion of the different topics. It's my pleasure to introduce the next sessions where we'll talk about the integration of sexual reproductive health and rights services through the work of midwives, and we'll focus on HIV AIDS service integration, family planning services and information, and addressing and identifying female genital mutilation.

And as you know, usually when we first talk about the role of midwives, the first thing that come into our mind is labor, childbirth, and pregnancy, but at the same time, midwives are the most trusted and accessible health force where they provide the full range of sexual reproductive health and rights and services. If you remember on day one yesterday, we heard how they can provide 90% of the full range of sexual reproductive health and rights information and services, so they play a role through providing HIV AIDS service integration, through testing, through prevention of mother to child transmission. They can also provide a role into counseling and information about family planning services, contraception during postpartum family planning, and also identifying women who are at risk and addressing their needs for those who are affected by female genital mutilation.

So specifically, midwives can play a role in three areas within this range. They can first ensure the integration of family planning services and information through the wider sexual reproductive health and rights. They can also provide the needed respected services to women and girls who are affected by female genital mutilation, and at the same time, they can help treat, diagnose, and identify women who are living with HIV.

But at the same time, it's not about just adding more services, not adding more responsibilities. It's about the wider system change. It's about education, continuous professional development, the availability of commodities, the referral pathway, and all of that sitting within an enabling policy environment.

So as we move forward, and we'll have the discussion and more from the experts, let us think together how to move from a fragmented service delivery to a more whole-of-system approach where midwives are enabled to provide the full range of sexual reproductive health and rights services and information in a qualitative, respectful way. And as we move forward into the discussion, then it's my pleasure to introduce my colleague, Dr. Chalanga Asmani, who will moderate the next panel discussion, and we'll hear from the experts from three countries. Thank you, and over to you.

Thank you. Thank you very much, Yusuf. So I think throughout day one, some of the common things that have been mentioned, and Yusuf has mentioned it today, is about how midwives can provide a holistic and a big range of SRHS services, how they are key contact to women and girls, and how they can provide integrated, holistic, and, obviously, person-centered care.

So that's what we've been hearing. What we want to do now is to hear from those that are on the ground what actually happens. Is this what happens? Are there successes? Are there challenges? And what can we do to ensure, really, we make best of this opportunity? So I'm going to invite three speakers, and what I would ask you, because the speakers are both English and French.
So for you in the audience, if you can have your headphones ready. And also, for the speakers who come up here, they are also available here. So we're going to have three.
The first one is Fatima Haridani. If you can please come up. And she's the president of the Komoro Island Midwifery Association and also represents the Federation of African Midwives.
Our second colleague is Hawa Abdulla Elmi from UNFPA Somalia. Please come forward. And we have our third, who is Annet Karyanyuzi from the National Midwifery Association of Uganda.
So please prepare with your headphones, because some questions will be in French. OK. OK.

So English is channel one, French is channel two, just so that when we transition from the different questions, you'll be able to access. So thank you very much. And we've talked about the holistic care.
We've talked about the potential. We've talked about what women and girls need. We've also talked about how it's important to provide the holistic, comprehensive, and women-centered care.

So now we want to ask from the reality, what goes from the experience of these three great ladies in front of us. So we'll start with from Uganda. If you could tell us, from the experience of Uganda, do you feel that your country, you know, midwives in Uganda, can we say that they seamlessly, I think here the keyword is seamlessly, deliver people-centered, comprehensive SRH and HIV services? You know, addressing adolescent health, family planning, maternal, and other gynecological services.

Do we find that it's happening seamlessly? Or how do you find it from the case of Uganda? Please share with us. Thank you so much, the moderator, and I'm delighted to share our experience from Uganda. And my answer is yes, with a however.

Uganda has made sustainable progress, but not yet seamlessly. When we look at the targets, the 95, 95, 95, we have had good progress. We are only struggling with the first 95, we are at 85% when it comes to testing for HIV.

That said, the unique role of midwives is grounded in the philosophy of diginity, compassionate care, a right-based, patient-centered approach, which is applicable to HIV, despite the dynamics that come with HIV. And in Uganda, our setting ranges from the lowest health center, at health center two to three, to a very super-specialized setting at the tertiary institution, and midwives are part and parcel of that care at all the stages. And midwives are central in providing HIV care and prevention and care along the four pillars for HIV prevention and care.

Midwives actively participate in antenatal, childbirth, postnatal, family planning, along the entire continuum of care. We are able to carry out the counseling, the testing, the linkages, especially the elimination of mother-to-child transmission has been our strongest contribution in Uganda as midwives. We also see that these contacts provide the opportunity for midwives to create a trusting relationship with the women and their partners.

You know, each time we are offering services, it's beyond a dispensing of services. There is a relationship that is built, and midwives are grounded in doing that. We also see that in Uganda, our HIV has mainly been, in the past, vertical.

The programming has been vertical, where you find everything is handled in the HIV clinics. The structures, the organization of care, the resourcing are all vertical. However, when it came to 2025 with the funding cuts, that got disrupted.
We saw a loss of previously supported staff by PEPFAR. We saw clinics closed. We saw a threat to continuity and availability of key resources, key supplies.

And the shift was transferred to the midwife to be the solution. And our government quickly intervened and brought in the concept of integrated service delivery, where the services now have to shift from the vertical programming to a bi-directional model, where we need to see services that were previously offered at HIV clinics now brought into the main clinic. And that definitely did come with its challenges.

For us to reflect is how well prepared were the midwives. And in our country, that was a challenge, because that meant additional workload. That meant an additional demand on reorganization of space for safe, confidential care.
And that didn't come easy. But above all, with HIV and its dynamics, we see the knowledge and skills gap. HIV is so dynamic.

It's rapidly evolving. And we are seeing a challenge in matching or aligning the knowledge and skills gap into this new assigned task for ensuring that there's seamless introduction of HIV care into our mainstream care. Thank you.
Okay. Thank you very much. Thank you.

Round of applause, please. I think it's a good description of what I took here is that the principle of midwifery really supports the whole aspect of providing dignified services. And I think when it comes to HIV, the stigma and other challenges that we've been seeing through, this is really an area where dignified services are required.

To an extent, we've seen where there's opportunity, where it has gone well. And we've also seen that the current changes, particularly in funding, have now put the limelight for that midwives have to do more. But what does this mean? It's more workload.

We need to rearrange what we're doing, where we're providing the services, the space, et cetera. But I think an important aspect when we think about the education, the training, and the support to midwives is about how this is also evolving. It's an ever-evolving disease.
There's over-evolving knowledge. And I think we need to look at these skills from the initial training up to the continuous training. So I think this is very key.

And thank you for that. So taking point on dignified services, the rights of women, we come to a very important aspect on the challenge we see when it comes to female genital mutilation. There's another area where we really have to seriously think, are we doing, are we protecting, and what else can we do? So I'd ask Amhawa from UNFES Somalia, from your point of view, where do you see midwives have a greatest opportunity to help prevent FGM and also support women and girls who have undergone it? How do we see this? Because we talk about midwives being able to provide this holistic care, midwives ensuring dignity.
And I think the challenge of FGM really requires this. So can you tell us how do you see midwives in this role? Yes, thank you so much. And thank you for organizing this important conversation.

And let me start with, we need to recognize that midwives have a unique role. And they are the first care providers for women who are at risk for FGM when it comes to prevention, and also providing quality care to women who already undergone FGM. So midwives, they have that unique role.

We need to recognize that they are not only, they are both attendants, but at the same time also, this gives them an opportunity that they can also influence families, challenge social norms, and also provide compassionate, confidential care and advocate the rights of women and girls. And in Somalia, where FGM still remains deeply rooted in social norms, and also we learned from Somalia that FGM and ending FGM requires more than campaigns. We need to engage communities, we need to empower midwives, and we need also to support transforming the health system to the way that it addresses FGM practice at the moment.

If I come back to your question, and midwives, to my experience, I'm happy that I'm talking today FGM, as a victim for FGM, as someone who provided other women suffering with FGM, and also as championing FGM zero tolerance in my country. And my experience teaches me or taught me that there are three important roles that midwives can play. The first one is prevention, because midwives have a unique role to during antenatal care, postnatal care, and also providing adolescent health services, and also engaging communities through community dialogue to provide prevention methods, messages, by changing the behavior and attitude of the community, educating them the consequence, both the long-term and short-term consequence of FGM.

And the second step or approach or area that midwives can also come on this FGM is providing quality care, because for women who already undergone FGM, midwives provide respectful and also confidential and self-centered care, including appropriate clinical management. In Somalia, 99% of Somali women already undergone, according to the Somali demographic health survey report, FGM. So they still need to be given care and treatment for managing the complication, managing their birth in the best, comfortable, and appropriate way to reduce the harm.

And also, in that moment, midwives still have the unique role. They can still provide prevention, especially first-time younger mothers who, soon after delivery, can better understand the complication of FGM and can pledge in that moment that they will never cut in their future girls or in their newborn baby girls. And the third one, I would like also to mention, it's about community engagement in Somalia.

We recognize the importance of working with religious leaders, fathers, especially engaging in the importance of male involvement, young people. Still, midwives can help connect messages through community dialogue to influence social norms. So I would like to stop key message that midwives should not only respond to the consequence of FGM, but also midwives must be empowered and supported to be the change of agents.
Thank you. Thank you very much. I think you brought a very important point where now we're looking at the role of midwives more largely.

You talked about not only being there to ensure safe delivery and safe birth, but here you talked about how, in this challenging harmful social norm, how we could think about the prevention aspect, the quality of care, the community engagement. So we see really the midwife as an all-rounded supporter of women's rights and dignity. That brings us to an important point.

This is what we expect of this midwife. So obviously, this midwife should have been trained, should have been supported, should continue to be mentored to provide this that we're saying, because it's quite a big package and about quite a big demand. So now I'd like to ask Fatima Alidani from Comoros something related to this.
How do we prepare these midwives? Can everybody? Okay. Okay, so I could ask the question in French for clarity. I hope everybody could listen in for the English translation.
Okay. So just put on your headphones while I prepare the question in French so that the panelists could get the question as it is. Are we good? Okay.
Merci beaucoup. Thank you very much. So at least here, we're trying to look at to get where we want to get.

What type of thinking do we need to rethink, improve, adapt, modify how we train our providers? So we're moving from siloed training because talk about integrated services. What about our training level? Are we also integrating? Are we also looking at these in silo? But also as the providers go out into the field and provide services, what else are we doing? Not only classroom, but how are we training on-site practical mentorship supervision? So this idea of integrated service could actually be realized. We need to rethink how we train from the basic to the continuous and to the supportive supervision.

So now if we go back to Annette, a number of words have been said. People-centered, women-centered. So looking at the situation in Uganda for Annette, what gaps or constraints or bottlenecks do you see when it comes to ensuring people-centered services by midwives from a systems, but also from a rights-based and community access perspective? Because this kept coming up.
So how do you look at it from your experience? Thank you so much, the moderator. And riding on my colleagues' submissions, Uganda is not so far away from what they're explaining. And it's clear.

Our experience shows that the principal constraint is not lack of commitment. Midwives are committed to seeing that we live in an HIV-free generation. The first and biggest constraint is in terms of human resource, like I already mentioned.
When we had the funding cuts, most of the PEPFAR-supported facilities lost over 50% of their staff. And that is quite a big challenge. But we also see midwives being unevenly distributed.

There's a rural-urban disparity with the hard-to-reach areas suffering the most. We have areas in the islands. We have areas in the mountainous regions where it's very complex and difficult to ensure that services are taken to the last mile, to the last mother in that farthest community.

Secondly, we see that there's overstretching of the midwives. Yes, the policy has been put in place, but we've not seen the filling of the staffing gaps. And the few midwives who are there are expected to do the antenatal, to do the postnatal, to do the follow-ups, to do everything.

And what does that end up into? Burnout and compromising quality of care for our clients. The other, of course, I had already mentioned, HIV requires a lot of tools, standard operating procedures, guidelines. They are good on paper, but not adequately disseminated.

Sometimes I ask, if I, the president, has not seen this police, is not aware of this police, what about my rural midwives in the island? It's because they've not been disseminated adequately due to the challenges that I've already mentioned. Some of these areas are hard to reach. Even when you put CPD sessions probably virtual, the same people are affected because there's no internet connection.
So the problems are quite dynamic. And that leaves unmatched competencies to the evolving changes. We have new introductions, for instance, the long-acting injectable for PrEP.

That's another opportunity, but still it requires capacity building, and still that has not been scaled to the last mile. Then another very critical, you know, HIV is interwoven into culture, socioeconomic, among other dynamics. So the client flows, commodity channels, reporting, are still, they need to be realigned to meet the diversities of our clients.

A woman may attend one facility, but also they need to be listened to, yet sometimes we are faced with language barrier. In Uganda, we have over 65 tribes. So are you able to disseminate the information to enable this client to understand? So client dynamics are a challenge, and they need to be addressed.

I talked about hard-to-reach areas, issues of access, issues of stigma, privacy issues are still a great challenge. Yes, we have the policies talking about integration, reorganization of care, but we do not see the aligned infrastructure development to suit the dynamics that I've talked about. Sometimes we also see restrictive social norms, especially among our adolescent clients.

In Uganda, recent statistics show that of the new infections, 70% are young girls. We are faced with early marriages, we are faced with sex for trade, we are faced with displacements due to disasters, and that worsens the HIV scenario, because girls are taken advantage of. So the question is, how best is this midwife prepared to answer these challenges? It's quite enormous on the midwife.

Thank you very much, and I think as we get to these points, as we go to our different group discussions, as we look at some of the actions that we need to take forward, let's look at what we wish for a midwife to be able to do, what our guidelines and our principles tell us midwives should do, but what are we hearing from the ground? But there's one thing you mentioned well, some things are on paper, what about in practice? What about the social-cultural dynamics of what the midwife has to overcome or deal with? So I think let's look at all of this so that we see how is this midwife trained to do what we wish them to do? How are they supported? How are the structure, the social-cultural environment, the community? I think the health systems infrastructure came out very clearly, but also as we look at this nice and comprehensive package, what does it mean in terms of the human resource capacity? Where are they located? Can every place, can every woman in every part of the country receive this package? Was there the urban-rural divide? And of course, where it's also hard to reach. So let's take these points as we think about actions that we need to do going forward. So I'll go back to how now, and I'll circle back to something important again we mentioned around training.

You mentioned around the role that a midwife needs to have in terms of the female genital mutilation prevention and treatment and management and support. So from your perspective, what should every midwife learn about FGM before they enter practice? And where do you see the biggest gap for this knowledge, for this attitude at the pre-service or in-service training, but also in doing supportive supervision? Because they need to have this at the basic entry, but also throughout all other learning opportunities. So how do you see midwives having a better way to learn about FGM and how to respond? Thank you.
Thank you so much. In short, to my experience, midwives need to have three important essential competencies. The first one is knowledge, and the second one is clinical skills.

And the third one is professional attitude, because these three usually matter. So they should understand and acknowledge the different types of FGM, as well as its consequence, so that they are able to explain the consequence and the communication, and they should know also how to provide appropriate survivor-centered, compassionate care to the women who already undergone FGM. From my experience in Somalia, it's that training alone is not enough.

And therefore, here we need to integrate survivor-centered competence into the pre-service midwifery curriculum. And I'm also making sure that a model dedicated on FGM is also included in the continuous professional development system, as well as clinical guidelines and protocols also should be there. So here we have key actors, the government, the Minister of Health.

We need also, we have also the health midwifery regulatory body that has also a unique role to ensure that those competence. So in this, no midwife should graduate from the school or from the university without knowing how to prevent the FGM, care for its survivors, as well as provide confidentially project this misconception of FGM practice. The other one is also the clinical, because we need also to manage communication.

And the third one is attitude, because we have the issue of medicalization of FGM. So the attitude and ethics of the midwife also matters when we are talking about FGM prevention. So here in Somalia, we in UNFPS Somalia, we supported the government to integrate into the private and public midwifery, pre-service midwifery training curriculum, as well as also supporting and advocating and encouraging the government that every midwife who graduates should pledge at her graduation that she will not perform FGM.

Because there is no FGM that is safe, even if it is performed by health professionals. And I can also confidently say that FGM medicalization is also a key reason that still FGM continues, because some communities, they believe that if FGM is performed by health professionals, it has less risk. So we need to empower midwives to challenge that misconception and advocate and jump beyond FGM zero tolerance.

Taking us also on a very important aspect, the comprehensiveness of the training. But I think another important aspect that I took in addition to how we need to ensure competence-based training, training itself is not enough. Talking about FGM as part of the continuous professional development, looking at the different curricula and the role of different actors.

But I think an important aspect that came is that while we talk about community outreach, when we talk about sensitization, we tend to talk about what providers or other people in the society go towards the community. But I think you mentioned an important point that us as a community of service providers like midwives, they also have to be sensitized on some of these important aspects, not to accept, as you said, even pledge that I will not perform FGM, not to accept that the myth that medically provide FGM is safe. So it means we also need to look inward in terms of the provider's attitude, which is very key.
So now I will go back to Fatima, and I'll ask the question in French. I'll ask, I think the third question that we had for you was also specific on family planning. So have your headsets ready.

Est-ce qu'il y a des obstacles? Quels sont ces obstacles? Qu'est-ce que vous recommande pour que vraiment les sages-femmes puissent offrir une grande gamme de services de planning familial à vous? Merci. Moi, je suis convaincue que les sages-femmes partout dans le monde, y compris mon pays, ont pleinement le potentiel et la légitimité clinique pour offrir une gamme complète et large des méthodes de planification familiale, y compris les méthodes réversibles à longue durée d'action, par exemple les implants, les divis, ainsi que l'auto-injection. D'ailleurs, c'est le cœur même de l'élargissement du champ de pratiques frôles par l'accélérateur de la pratique des sages-femmes.

Cependant, plusieurs obstacles freinent encore cette pleine autonomie dans la plupart des pays. Par exemple, des cadres réglementaires parfois restrictifs ou fragmentés qui ne reflètent pas les compétences relatives par les sages-femmes. Dans certains pays, la sage-femme est formée, par exemple, je dis bien par exemple, à poser un implant, mais la loi ne lui autorise pas d'insérer.

Il y a aussi un déficit d'investissement dans les environnements de travail avec manque d'équipement, une instabilité de l'approvisionnement de contraceptives dans les centres périphériques. Exemple, dans notre pays actuellement, au Comoros, nous avons des ruptures de certains produits contraceptifs. Donc, la femme est obligée d'aller dans les pharmacies chercher quelle méthode elle peut en avoir pour espacer ses naissances.

Ça peut arriver que cette méthode ne lui plaît pas, mais elle est obligée ou ne va pas avec sa santé, si elle est tendue ou bien diabétique. Donc, il y a aussi les barrières socio-culturelles et le manque de données désagrégées permettant de suivre l'impact des sages-femmes sur la couverture contraceptive. Donc, pour surmonter ces obstacles, j'ai fourni trois recommandations clés, alignées peut-être dans notre feuille de route.

Un, actualiser les cadres réglementaires afin d'autoriser explicitement les sages-femmes à prescrire et administrer l'ensemble des méthodes de planification familiale au niveau primaire en harmonie avec les normes de l'OMS et de l'ISER. Deuxièmement, sécuriser le financement domestique et la chaîne logistique en intégrant pleinement le produit de santé reproductif, les besoins des sages-femmes dans le budget national de santé et le mécanisme de couverture sanitaire universel. Et ma troisième recommandation, c'est de renforcer le leadership des sages-femmes et l'engagement communautaire en impliquant nos associations professionnelles dans la gouvernance et en travaillant la main dans la main avec les leaders communautaires et religieux.
Nous pourrons lever les barrières sociales. Merci. Thank you.

Thank you very much. So, when I come back to how Youssef introduced the fact that we've been hearing over the last two days, midwives can provide 90 plus of all the SHR services. But these, if you list these services and you list what the regulation allows them to do or not, is there a match? Was there a mismatch? Can they actually provide this big set of services? So I think there's some policy work, regulation work that we need to do, and I think that's part of the things we're discussing.

So to close, because we have just four minutes left, I'd like to ask from the left, going to the right, what one thing do you want to advocate for the group work as people go into groups to ensure they do not forget what is needed to ensure that midwives can actually provide this comprehensive SRH set of services? Just think of one thing so that in the groups they take this into account and it comes in our call to action. So starting with you, Annette, one thing that you did not forget to make this happen, to make comprehensive SRH service delivery by midwives a possibility. Thank you so much.

There's no doubt that midwives have the potential to deliver HIV packages. However, we've seen there's a misalignment with the capacity to do that. So I would propose we define a minimum integrated midwifery service package at every level of care to ensure continuity of care for the patients.

And this is based on the midwives' distinct contribution and ability to connect clinical prevention with informed choice, respectful care, family planning, community engagement, and follow-up should all be maximized in that package that we are talking about. Thank you. And Fatima, for you, what key message do you want the group to try to integrate in the SRH? In my experience in my country, I would say that midwives should really get closer to the community.
And it is this community itself that will be their lawyer for the debtors of all they owe. Okay. Over to you, Hawa.

Yeah. My mind is short. Let us not recognize that midwives, they are frontline providers for integrated SRH and also GDV prevention, but let us invest in them to be the leaders for the movement to ensure that no one is left behind.
Thank you. Okay. Thank you very much.

A big round of applause to our three experts. I think they really helped us to bring what we talk about, what is global, what is guidance, to what is actually on the ground. So we want them to deliver, but we need to provide them the capacity.

We'll talk about advocacy. We could have the community women themselves advocate for what we want from the midwives so that we listen to them as those that receive services. And then also, let's think about making midwives as leaders, as advocates going forward to advance this.

So really, thank you for these three excellent perspectives, and thank you for your attention. And while our panelists have their wonderful photo taken, I'm very excited to announce to you all that it's now time for lunch, and today that's not a trick. So there are tokens for you for lunch at the registration desk.

You have a full hour for lunch, and after lunch, we have another session, so please come back here afterwards. If you have not yet put in your votes for Accelerator One Actions, this is your last chance, so be sure to scan this QR code, because when we come back later, we're moving on to the next accelerator. So thank you all so much.
Please enjoy your lunch, and we'll see you back here in an hour. Thanks.
